title: Name It, Carry It, Contain It: Specimen ID, Transport and Biosafety
summary: Label microbiology specimens with two identifiers and an exact source, choose the right swab transport, know when a safety cabinet and BSL-3 practices are needed, and recognise and refer a suspected Francisella tularensis isolate.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 66 Hits 15 (F. tularensis culture), 32 (bedside labelling with two identifiers), 33 (Amies/Stuart swab transport) and 34 (BSC, BSL-2 vs BSL-3). Checked against the ASM sentinel guideline for F. tularensis (2016 PDF, read in full), the CDC 2012 MMWR safe-work-practices guideline (read on the CDC web page), IDSA/ASM 2013 (Baron), Lippi 2017, Ning 2016, Mesganaw 2024, Hubbard 2011, Gavina 2023, Carvalho 2014 and 42 CFR 493.1242 (eCFR). Qualified: “no growth on sheep blood agar” and “3–5 days” (scant growth; 1–2 mm after ≥ 48 h); “never pre-label tubes” (CLSI says label after filling, WHO and SIBioC before, EFLM by local risk analysis); BSL-3 applies to TB decontamination and culture work, not every TB specimen step; for suspected Francisella the stricter ASM wording (Class II BSC with BSL-3 precautions) is taught. Not taught: “transport media stop multiplication” (Van Horn 2008 page was blocked by a browser check), “eye protection for every specimen”. The refrigeration rules for gonococcal and anaerobic swabs are taught in micro-specimen-acceptability-transport.

objectives: Apply two-identifier, bedside labelling with a specific specimen source, and explain why rules on pre-labelling differ.
Choose the correct swab transport device and temperature for routine and gonococcal culture swabs.
Decide when a specimen or culture needs a biological safety cabinet or BSL-3 practices.
Recognise the culture clues of Francisella tularensis and the sentinel-laboratory response.

scenes.title: Three arrivals at the night bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three items reach the microbiology receiving bench at night: (1) a blood tube with no label, sent with a requisition and a note “labelled later at the station”; (2) a wound swab in an Amies gel transport tube; (3) a lymph node aspirate from a febrile rabbit hunter, with the request “rule out tularaemia”. Question token: “Accept it? Carry it how? Open it where?”

cues.text: Three arrivals at the night bench. A blood tube with no label, sent with a note saying it will be labelled later at the nurses’ station.
A wound swab in an Amies transport tube. And a lymph node aspirate from a rabbit hunter with fever, marked: rule out tularaemia.
Should the lab accept it, how should it travel, and where may it be opened?

props.label: Accept it? Carry it how? Open it where?

scenes.title: Naming the specimen
scenes.altText: Schematic: a patient wristband and a specimen tube. Card 1 (Joint Commission goal as summarised by Lippi 2017): use at least two patient identifiers when collecting specimens; room number or location is never an identifier; label containers in the presence of the patient. A European working group recommends at least two, preferably three, identifiers, one being the full name. Card 2 (US CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1242): the laboratory must have written procedures for specimen labelling, including patient name or a unique identifier and, when appropriate, the specimen source. Card 3 (IDSA/ASM 2013): a label such as “wound” or “eye” is not enough; give the specific site, for example “dog bite wound, right forefinger”.

cues.text: A specimen is only useful if it belongs, beyond doubt, to one patient. The Joint Commission goal asks for at least two patient identifiers when specimens are collected, such as full name and date of birth or record number.
A room or bed number is never an identifier, and the container is labelled in the presence of the patient. A European working group asks for at least two, preferably three, identifiers.
In the United States, CLIA requires written labelling procedures that include the patient’s name or a unique identifier and, when appropriate, the specimen source.
In microbiology the source must be specific: not just wound, but dog bite wound, right forefinger.

props.title: Who is it from?
lines: Label in front of the patient

scenes.title: When to label, how to carry, where to open
scenes.altText: Card 1, “When to label?”: guidance differs. CLSI venipuncture procedure: label tubes after filling. WHO and the Italian society SIBioC: label before filling. EFLM working group: check identity in the patient’s presence and decide before-or-after by local risk analysis (Lippi 2017). One hospital’s restrictive acceptance policy did not allow relabelling of unlabelled or mislabelled specimens, except irretrievable ones such as CSF, tissue or pre-antibiotic blood cultures, which needed the collector to come to the lab and sign (Ning 2016). Card 2, “How to carry?” (IDSA/ASM 2013): a swab for aerobic culture goes in a swab transport device at room temperature within 2 hours, flocked swabs recommended; a gonococcal culture swab goes in Amies or Stuart medium at room temperature, or Amies with charcoal. Liquid Amies and Stuart are nutrient-poor transport media; over long, non-ideal storage, counts can still drift up or down (Hubbard 2011). Card 3, “Where to open?” (CDC 2012): the general clinical microbiology laboratory works at BSL-2, using a biological safety cabinet (BSC) for specimen processing and any work that makes aerosols or splashes, with coats, gloves and face protection as needed; isolates of small gram-negative coccobacilli are manipulated in the BSC, and sniffing culture plates is prohibited.

cues.text: When should the tube be labelled? Guidance differs. The CLSI venipuncture procedure labels after filling, while WHO and an Italian society label before. A European group leaves it to local risk analysis, but identity is always checked with the patient present.
One hospital’s strict policy refused to relabel unlabelled specimens, except irretrievable ones such as CSF, tissue or pre-antibiotic blood cultures, and then only with the collector present to sign.

How should it travel? A culture swab goes in a swab transport device at room temperature, ideally within two hours. Gonococcal culture swabs use Amies or Stuart medium, or Amies with charcoal. These media are nutrient-poor, yet over long storage counts can still drift.

Where may it be opened? The routine clinical lab works at biosafety level two, using a safety cabinet for specimen processing and anything that splashes or makes aerosols. Small gram-negative coccobacilli are handled in the cabinet, and plates are never sniffed.

props.title: Where to open? (BSL-2)
lines: Coat, gloves, face shield as needed

scenes.title: When the agent raises the level
scenes.altText: Card 1, tuberculosis (CDC 2012): specimens submitted for TB testing are handled in a BSC with coat and gloves; procedures that do not make aerosols can be done at BSL-2; specimen decontamination, culture propagation and culture manipulation are done at BSL-3. Dimorphic moulds: BSL-3 practices for mould-form cultures of Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Paracoccidioides; never use petri plates if Coccidioides is suspected. Card 2, Francisella tularensis (ASM sentinel guideline 2016): patient specimens are handled in a Class II BSC, at BSL-3 or at BSL-2 with BSL-3 precautions (the guideline also says clinical specimens can be processed with BSL-2 practices); once the Gram stain or culture suggests F. tularensis, all manipulation is done in the BSC with BSL-3 practices; plates are taped shut. Tiny, faintly staining gram-negative coccobacilli; scant growth on sheep blood agar (it may fail to grow on subculture because it needs cysteine); on chocolate agar, colonies are usually too small to see at 24 hours and about 1–2 mm after 48 hours or more; no growth on MacConkey; oxidase negative, catalase negative or weak, beta-lactamase positive, no satellite growth; plates for tissue held 7 days; no commercial or automated identification systems including MALDI-TOF; refer to the LRN reference laboratory. Hook answers: (1) unlabelled blood tube: reject and recollect; (2) Amies swab: room temperature, fine for culture; (3) node aspirate: alert the lab, process the specimen in a Class II BSC with BSL-3 precautions, and keep all further work there once the smear or growth looks like Francisella.

cues.text: Some agents raise the level. Tuberculosis specimens are opened in the safety cabinet with coat and gloves. Decontamination and culture work move to biosafety level three, as do mould-form cultures of the dimorphic fungi.

Francisella tularensis: the sentinel guideline asks for patient specimens to be handled in a class two cabinet with level-three precautions, and once a tiny, faint gram-negative coccobacillus appears, all further work stays there. Growth on blood agar is scant, colonies on chocolate reach one to two millimetres after forty-eight hours, and MacConkey stays empty.
It is oxidase negative and beta-lactamase positive, and it shows no satellite growth. Tissue plates are held seven days, and automated systems, including MALDI-TOF, are not used. Refer it.

Back to the hook. Reject and recollect the unlabelled tube. The Amies swab travels at room temperature. The node aspirate is processed in the cabinet with level-three precautions, and all further work stays there once the smear or growth looks suspicious.

props.title: Suspect F. tularensis
lines: Blood agar scant · choc 1–2 mm ≥ 48 h

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Relabel the unlabelled tube at the bench” (✓ reject and recollect; any exception for an irretrievable specimen follows written policy with the collector present); “No growth on blood agar rules out Francisella” (✓ it grows scantly or not at all on blood agar; use chocolate or cysteine media and wait 48 hours or more); “All TB work needs a BSL-3 room” (✓ specimens are opened in a BSC; decontamination and culture work need BSL-3).

cues.text: Trap one: relabel an unlabelled tube at the bench. No. Reject it and recollect. An irretrievable specimen is handled only under written policy.
Trap two: poor growth on blood agar rules out Francisella. No. It grows scantly there; it needs cysteine-rich media such as chocolate, and forty-eight hours or more.
Trap three: every step of tuberculosis work needs a level-three room. No. Specimens are opened in a safety cabinet; decontamination and culture work need level three.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Two identifiers, labelled with the patient present · specific source · right transport device”, “BSL-2 with a cabinet for specimens · BSL-3 practices for TB cultures and suspected Francisella isolates”.

cues.text: Label every specimen with two identifiers in front of the patient, send it in the right transport device, and open it in a safety cabinet, moving to level-three practices for tuberculosis cultures and suspected Francisella tularensis.

props.label: 2 identifiers, patient present · exact source · right device
BSC for specimens · BSL-3 for TB cultures and Francisella

explanation.what: Plain language: before testing, the lab must be sure whose specimen it is and where it came from, it must arrive alive in the right container, and it must be opened where it cannot infect the staff. Scientific terms: patient identifiers, specimen source, restrictive acceptance policy, irretrievable specimen, swab transport device, Amies and Stuart media, biological safety cabinet (BSC), biosafety level (BSL) 2 and 3, sentinel laboratory, Laboratory Response Network (LRN), Francisella tularensis.
explanation.why: Identification errors arise in the pre-analytical phase, before any test is run; organism counts can change in transport media during long or poor storage; and laboratory exposures, including unrecognised aerosols, happen more often than is generally suspected, so containment is matched to the agent and to whether a culture is being handled.
explanation.measure: At least two identifiers (never room or bed); label in the patient’s presence; specific source. Culture swab: transport device, room temperature, ideally ≤ 2 h; gonococcal culture swab in Amies or Stuart (Amies with charcoal), room temperature. BSL-2 with a BSC for specimen processing and aerosol or splash work; TB decontamination and culture work at BSL-3; suspected F. tularensis specimen or isolate: Class II BSC with BSL-3 precautions or practices, taped plates, chocolate agar 1–2 mm colonies after ≥ 48 h, scant on blood agar, none on MacConkey, oxidase negative, beta-lactamase positive, no satellitism, tissue plates 7 days, no automated identification, refer to LRN.
explanation.differs: TB specimen vs TB culture (BSL-2 with BSC for non-aerosol steps vs BSL-3); retrievable vs irretrievable specimen (recollect vs policy exception); F. tularensis vs Haemophilus influenzae (no satellite growth, beta-lactamase positive).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the acceptable identifier pair, what to do with an unlabelled specimen, where to process a suspected TB or tularaemia specimen, which plate grows F. tularensis, and why MALDI-TOF is avoided for a suspected select agent.

questions.stem: A lymph node aspirate from a rabbit hunter grows tiny colonies on chocolate agar at 72 hours, scant growth on blood agar and nothing on MacConkey. The Gram stain shows tiny, faint gram-negative coccobacilli. What should the sentinel laboratory do next?

options.text: Tape the plates, work only in a Class II BSC with BSL-3 practices, and refer to the LRN reference laboratory
options.rationale: Correct. The ASM sentinel guideline moves suspected F. tularensis into the BSC with BSL-3 practices and refers it for confirmation.

options.text: Identify the colony by MALDI-TOF or an automated panel
options.rationale: Incorrect. Automated and commercial systems risk aerosols and misidentification and are not used for a suspected F. tularensis isolate.

options.text: Report no pathogen, because it barely grows on blood agar
options.rationale: Incorrect. Scant growth on blood agar is expected; the organism needs cysteine-rich media such as chocolate agar.

options.text: Subculture on the open bench and sniff the plate for odour
options.rationale: Incorrect. Colonies are manipulated only in a BSC, and sniffing plates is prohibited.

questions.stem: Which of these may NOT be used as one of the two patient identifiers when labelling a specimen?

options.text: The patient’s room and bed number
options.rationale: Correct. Room number or physical location is never an identifier.
Incorrect. Full name is a standard identifier.
Incorrect. Date of birth is an accepted identifier.
Incorrect. A medical record number is an accepted identifier.

questions.stem: A sputum specimen is submitted for tuberculosis testing. Which handling matches the CDC 2012 safe-work-practices guidance?

options.text: Open it in a BSC wearing coat and gloves; do decontamination and culture work at BSL-3
options.rationale: Correct. TB specimens are handled in a BSC, and decontamination, culture propagation and manipulation are BSL-3 work.

options.text: Open it on the open bench if the technologist wears a surgical mask
options.rationale: Incorrect. TB specimens are opened in a BSC; a mask does not replace containment.

options.text: Refuse it unless a BSL-4 laboratory is available
options.rationale: Incorrect. BSL-4 is for exotic agents with high individual risk; TB culture work is BSL-3.

options.text: Only the final culture report needs precautions
options.rationale: Incorrect. Precautions apply from the moment the specimen is opened.

Clin Infect Dis. 2013;57(4):e22-e121. doi:10.1093/cid/cit278
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Specimens must be labelled accurately and completely; specific source (“dog bite wound right forefinger”, not “wound” or “eye”); Table Introduction-1: aerobic culture swab in swab transport device, room temperature, 2 h, flocked swabs recommended; gonococcal culture swab in Amies or Stuart transport medium at room temperature (rectal, 8 h) and Amies charcoal transport at room temperature.

Joint Commission NPSG.01.01.01: at least two patient identifiers when collecting specimens; room number or location not an identifier; label containers in the presence of the patient; EFLM WG-PRE: at least two (preferably three) identifiers, one the full name; CLSI venipuncture procedure labels tubes after filling, WHO and SIBioC before filling, EFLM by local risk analysis; labelling error types.

references.citation: Ning HC, Lin CN, Chiu DT, et al. Reduction in Hospital-Wide Clinical Laboratory Specimen Identification Errors following Process Interventions: A 10-Year Retrospective Observational Study. PLoS One. 2016;11(8):e0160821. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0160821
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. At least two identifiers before collection; labels attached at the time of collection; restrictive acceptance policy: no relabelling of mislabelled or unlabelled specimens except irretrievable ones (CSF, tissue, pre-antibiotic blood cultures), which required the collector to come to the laboratory and sign.

references.citation: Hubbard K, Pellar G, Emanuel P. Suitability of Commercial Transport Media for Biological Pathogens under Nonideal Conditions. Int J Microbiol. 2011;2011:463096. doi:10.1155/2011/463096
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Liquid Amies and Stuart are nutrient-poor commercial transport media; over extended storage under non-ideal conditions they did not keep an accurate representation of the organism quantity collected (counts rose for one organism and fell for another).

references.citation: Gavina K, Whitacre BE, Meyer TL, et al. The Brief Case: Suspicious Gram-Negative Coccobacilli-Francisella tularensis subsp. novicida Isolated from an Immunocompromised Patient. J Clin Microbiol. 2023;61(6):e0078722. doi:10.1128/jcm.00787-22

references.citation: Carvalho CL, Lopes de Carvalho I, Zé-Zé L, Núncio MS, Duarte EL. Tularaemia: a challenging zoonosis. Comp Immunol Microbiol Infect Dis. 2014;37(2):85-96. doi:10.1016/j.cimid.2014.01.002

claims.text: At least two identifiers; room or location never an identifier; label in the patient’s presence; EFLM two, preferably three.
US CLIA requires written labelling procedures with name or unique identifier and, when appropriate, source.
Specific anatomic source on the label.
CLSI labels after filling; WHO and SIBioC before; EFLM by local risk analysis.

Problems with patient identification are a rejection criterion and rejected specimens usually need recollection; restrictive acceptance: no relabelling except irretrievable specimens under policy (one hospital).

Swab transport device at room temperature within 2 h, flocked swabs; gonococcal culture swab in Amies or Stuart (Amies charcoal); Amies and Stuart are nutrient-poor; counts drift over long non-ideal storage.

BSL-2 with BSC for processing and aerosol work; small gram-negative coccobacilli in the BSC; no sniffing plates; TB specimen in BSC, decontamination and culture at BSL-3; dimorphic mould cultures BSL-3; no petri plates for Coccidioides.

F. tularensis: patient specimens in a Class II BSC with BSL-3 precautions, all further manipulation there once suspected; scant on blood agar, 1–2 mm on chocolate after ≥ 48 h, none on MacConkey; oxidase −, beta-lactamase +, no satellitism; tissue plates 7 days; no automated identification; refer to LRN.

Reviewer’s “transport media keep organisms alive without letting them multiply”, “eye protection for all specimens”, “no growth on sheep blood agar, pinpoint colonies in 3–5 days” and “never pre-label tubes”.
claims.note: Not taught as facts. The swab-transport validation paper (Van Horn 2008) was blocked by a browser check and could not be read; the other points are contradicted or qualified by the sources read (see accuracy flags).

claims.text: Scenario invented; tubes, swabs, plates and cabinet schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 66 Hit 15 says F. tularensis shows no growth on sheep blood agar and pinpoint colonies on chocolate agar in 3–5 days. The ASM sentinel guideline (2016) says it may grow at first on blood agar (scant growth) but can fail on subculture because it needs cysteine, and that chocolate-agar colonies are usually too small to see at 24 h but about 1–2 mm after 48 h or more; Gavina 2023 also describes scant growth on blood agar at 48 h. The 7-day hold is supported for tissue specimens. The lesson teaches the guideline wording. (register flag rv-ch66-ftularensis-growth).

Ch. 66 Hit 32 says never pre-label tubes. Lippi 2017 reports that the CLSI venipuncture procedure labels tubes after filling, but WHO and the Italian society SIBioC require labelling before filling, and the EFLM working group leaves the choice to local risk analysis while always checking identity in the patient’s presence. The lesson teaches that guidance differs (register flag rv-ch66-prelabel-guidance).

Ch. 66 Hit 32 says an unlabelled or mislabelled specimen is rejected and recollected. That is correct for recollectable specimens, but restrictive acceptance policies can allow documented exceptions for irretrievable specimens (CSF, tissue, pre-antibiotic blood cultures), with the collector identifying the specimen in person (Ning 2016, one hospital).

Ch. 66 Hit 34 places suspected tuberculosis, dimorphic fungi and select agents at BSL-3 without separating specimens from cultures. CDC 2012 allows non-aerosol procedures on TB specimens at BSL-2 (in a BSC, coat and gloves), with decontamination, culture propagation and culture manipulation at BSL-3, and recommends BSL-3 practices and facilities for mould-form cultures of dimorphic fungi. For F. tularensis the ASM sentinel guideline is itself mixed (Section II.A: clinical specimens can be processed with BSL-2 practices; Section II.B: all patient specimens in BSL-3 or BSL-2 with BSL-3 precautions in a Class II BSC), so the lesson teaches the stricter wording (register flag rv-ch66-bsl3-specimen-vs-culture).

The identification, labelling and biosafety rules taught here come from US (Joint Commission, CLIA, CDC, ASM sentinel/LRN) and European sources. Philippine rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.

morphology.note: No micrographs or plate photographs; specimens, plates and cabinet are schematic cards.
